# ⚙️ 01 · The Machine

**Nothing on this page is typed twice.** Every number you have seen so far, and every picture below, is the output of a workflow that runs on a crontab. This is that crontab, drawn from the workflow files themselves:

</div>

<picture>
  <source media="(prefers-color-scheme: dark)" srcset="./assets/art-pulse-aurora.svg?v=2027a">
  <source media="(prefers-color-scheme: light)" srcset="./assets/art-pulse-daylight.svg?v=2027a">
  <img src="./assets/art-pulse-aurora.svg?v=2027a" width="1160" height="560" alt="Heartbeat wheel: 24 hours on the clock face, one hand per workflow run, with a ledger of every cron line and its runs per day.">
</picture>

### What each bot does

| automation | schedule (UTC) | what it produces | fails how |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **skyline** | hourly, `:07` | `assets/data/snapshot.json`: commits, repos, streak, followers — the single source every other sheet reads | falls back to the last cache and writes nothing |
| **pulse** | `:23` every 4h | the clock above, by re-reading the cron lines of all 12 workflows | drawing only, so it cannot fail on the network |
| **ledger** | `:31` at 01/07/13/19 | the commit fan and the facts sheet | pure local Python |
| **live** | `:11` every 2h | two HTTPS probes per app, latency bar, content fingerprint | catches its own errors and draws them red |
| **findings** | `:47` every 3h | six hygiene checks across every repository | opens an issue if it finds a committed `.env`, never edits other repos |
| **postcard** | `:17` every 6h | the postcard wall, from real GitHub issues | marker-guarded; skips itself if the README has no slot |
| **state** | `:53` at 05/17 | the five headline numbers | reads local files only |
| **daybreak** | `:37` at 02 | one line a day: what actually happened | publishes "no commits" when there were none |
| **healthcheck** | `:29` at 04 | runs every generator against mock data and fails the build if any of them breaks | this is the one that protects the rest |

### Why the old version kept losing commits

The previous edition had each bot commit and push on its own. Several schedules fired in the same minute, so one push would win and the other would die with `Updates were rejected`. Two fixes went in:

```diff
-  git commit -m "chore: refresh" && git push        # loses the race, silently
+  bash .github/scripts/commit.sh "chore: refresh"   # rebase, retry, never give up
```

1. **one serialiser** — every bot writes through [`commit.sh`](./.github/scripts/commit.sh): stage, rebase on `origin`, commit, push, and on rejection reset and rebuild the commit on top of the winner instead of dying. Backoff, five tries.
2. **one writer per file** — each sheet owns its own `assets/data/*.json` and its own SVG names, so no workflow ever rewrites another's output and the rebase is always trivial.

There is a third property worth naming: **the pipeline verifies itself**. [`doctor.py`](./.github/scripts/doctor.py) checks that every asset the README references exists, that every marker pair appears exactly once, that every SVG parses and carries no script or external URL, that the cron counts on disk match the counts printed in the README, and that no relative link is dead. `healthcheck.yml` runs it nightly with `--strict`.

<summary><b>The full pipeline, as one sequence</b></summary>

<br>

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant C as crontab
    participant W as runner
    participant S as skyline.py
    participant A as api.github.com
    participant D as assets/data
    participant G as commit.sh
```

# 🧭 02 · Two Apps, In Production

</div>

### 🛍️ Aurevyn — a storefront with an operations team

A resale storefront (Meesho-style) built on Next.js + PostgreSQL, with an admin console and a small set of autonomous jobs that keep inventory and prices tidy. Still in progress — and the only project on this profile where the automation idea from *this* page is the product itself.

| layer | choice | why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| web | Next.js App Router, TypeScript | server components keep the storefront cheap on a phone-built codebase |
| data | PostgreSQL, schema-first | the admin console and the storefront must read the same truth |
| auth | session cookies, hashed passwords | no token in `localStorage`, ever |
| jobs | scheduled scripts in-repo | same philosophy as this profile: small Python, no mystery |

### ⚡ NexusMart — the one that taught me security

A full-stack store: JWT auth with bcrypt and HTTP-only cookies, cart and checkout, a role-gated admin panel, and Zod validation on every mutation.

The lesson worth repeating: **a ₹1 test order is cheaper than an audit**. When I probed my own checkout with a manipulated price, the server accepted it. The fix was not a UI check — it was moving the price computation server-side and validating the cart total against the database before payment. That is the difference between a demo and a product.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    actor U as visitor
    participant F as Next.js route
    participant V as zod schema
    participant DB as mongo / postgres
    participant P as payment

    U->>F: POST /api/checkout {items, claimedTotal}
    F->>V: parse every field
    V-->>F: typed cart or 400
    F->>DB: price each item server-side
    F->>V: compare recomputed total to claimedTotal
    alt totals disagree
        F-->>U: 409 — cart repriced, nothing charged
    else totals agree
        F->>P: charge the recomputed amount
        P-->>F: receipt
        F-->>U: 201 + order id
    end
```

<br>

```mermaid
erDiagram

    ORDER ||--|{ ORDER_ITEM : contains
    PRODUCT ||--o{ ORDER_ITEM : "sold as"
    PRODUCT }o--|| CATEGORY : "filed under"
    USER ||--o{ REVIEW : writes
    PRODUCT ||--o{ REVIEW : receives

    USER {
        string id PK
        string email UK
        string password_hash

    }
    PRODUCT {
        string id PK
        string title
        int price_paise
        int stock
    }

        string id PK

        int total_paise
        string status
    }
```

<a name="live"></a>

# 🛰️ 04 · Live, Right Now

Two HTTPS requests per app, every two hours, with the better latency kept. A fingerprint of the first 8 KiB tells us whether the page itself changed, not just whether it answered.

</div>

<picture>
  <source media="(prefers-color-scheme: dark)" srcset="./assets/live-aurora.svg?v=2027a">
  <source media="(prefers-color-scheme: light)" srcset="./assets/live-daylight.svg?v=2027a">
  <img src="./assets/live-aurora.svg?v=2027a" width="1160" height="342" alt="Live probe: status codes, latency bars, server and content fingerprints for each deployed app.">
</picture>

<details>
<summary><b>What the fingerprint actually buys</b></summary>

<br>

A status code tells you a server answered. It does not tell you the server answered *the right thing* — an outage page is a 200. Hashing the response body means a deploy is visible here even when nothing is red:

| change | what you see | what it means |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `200 → 200`, new fingerprint | shape changes, `repeat` resets to 1 | a deploy landed |
| `200 → 200`, same fingerprint | `repeat` climbs | the page is stable for N runs |
| `200 → 5xx` | status turns red | real downtime; the workflow stays green |
| timeout twice | `0 ms` and red | the probe records the miss instead of hiding it |

</details>

<img src="./assets/art-divider-aurora.svg?v=2027a" width="1160" height="44" alt="chapter divider">

<div align="center">
<a name="review"></a>

# 🔍 05 · The Bot Reviews Its Own Work

`findings.py` walks the root of every repository I own and checks six things that actually break projects: a README, a `.gitignore`, a licence, CI, tests, and a dependency manifest — plus one thing that should never happen: a committed `.env`.

The score below is **allowed to go down**. If a check fails, it is printed, not hidden. A percentage that can only rise is decoration.

| check | what counts | why it matters |
| --- | --- | --- |
| readme | any `README*` at the root | a repo nobody can understand is a repo nobody uses |
| gitignore | `.gitignore` present | `node_modules`, `.env`, editor droppings |
| licence | `LICENSE` / `LICENCE` / `COPYING` | without it, "public" is not the same as "usable" |
| ci | `.github/workflows` or a pipeline file | if it is never run, nobody knows when it is broken |
| tests | `tests/`, `__tests__/`, `*.test.*`, `test_*.py` | a learning project may skip these; a product may not |
| manifest | `package.json`, `pyproject.toml`, `requirements*.txt` | pinned dependencies are reproducible dependencies |

> The honest note: several of my early learning repositories were pushed before I understood why these things exist. The point of scoring them is not the number — it is that the next repository starts at six out of six by default.

# 📱 06 · The Phone

I do not own a laptop. Everything here — the art, the Python, the workflows, this sentence — is written on an Android phone, in [Termux](https://termux.dev) and GitHub's web editor.

```diff
- excuse:  "I'll start when I get a laptop."
+ reality: 2 apps in production, 9 automations, 14 SVGs, one phone.
```

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Termux
    Termux --> git : clone, branch, commit
    git --> editor : GitHub web editor for the big edits
    editor --> push : push from Termux
    push --> Actions : the workflows wake up
    Actions --> sheets : SVGs and JSON regenerate
    sheets --> Termux : pull the result
    Termux --> [*] : next idea
    note right of Actions
        9 scheduled workflows
        65 runs a day
    end note
```

The constraint shaped the whole design of this page. No local build server, so the art is generated where it can run: in GitHub Actions, on Python's standard library, with no dependencies to install.

<img src="./assets/art-divider-aurora.svg?v=2027a" width="1160" height="44" alt="chapter divider">

# 🎨 07 · The Craft — How These Pictures Exist

Every SVG on this page is drawn by a Python module in [`art/`](./art). No design tools, no icon packs, no bitmaps except nothing at all. The whole set is deterministic: same inputs, same bytes, which is why `healthcheck.yml` can fail the moment a drawing drifts.

| module | draws | why it exists |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [`kit.py`](./art/kit.py) | the two palettes, escaping, arcs, a deterministic star field | one place for every colour, so the two themes cannot drift |
| [`header.py`](./art/header.py) | the identity plate and the commit skyline | a header that reports instead of decorating |
| [`pulse.py`](./art/pulse.py) | the heartbeat wheel | it *parses* the cron lines rather than repeating them |
| [`divider.py`](./art/divider.py) | the chapter rule | nineteen of them, 1.3 KB each |
| [`ledger.py`](./.github/scripts/ledger.py) | the feathered commit fan | a count turned into a shape people actually read |

Rebuild all of it with one command — data, sheets, README regions, then the checks:

```bash
python3 art/universe.py                 # everything, in the order the workflows use
python3 art/build_all.py --only pulse   # or one sheet, both themes
python3 art/preview.py                  # rasterise to artifacts/ for eyeballing
```

<details>
<summary><b>Why two themes, and how it is wired</b></summary>

<br>

GitHub re-renders Markdown images with the visitor's colour scheme, so every sheet is drawn twice and selected by a `<picture>` element:

```html
<picture>
  <source media="(prefers-color-scheme: dark)"  srcset="./assets/art-pulse-aurora.svg?v=2027a">
  <source media="(prefers-color-scheme: light)" srcset="./assets/art-pulse-daylight.svg?v=2027a">
  <img src="./assets/art-pulse-aurora.svg?v=2027a" width="1160" height="560" alt="…">
</picture>
```

The `?v=2027a` query is the cache key. When a sheet changes, the version moves and every browser fetches the new file instead of a stale copy from the image CDN.

</details>

<img src="./assets/art-divider-aurora.svg?v=2027a" width="1160" height="44" alt="chapter divider">

<div align="center">
<a name="faq"></a>

# 💬 FAQ

</div>

<details>
<summary><b>Is any of this fake?</b></summary>

<br>

No. Every number is read from the GitHub API or from local files that a workflow wrote. If a probe fails, it is drawn red; if a repository has no tests, the hygiene score drops. The one number this page deliberately does **not** show is "commits per second" — a 1 commit per second average is under 2% of the profile's lifetime total, so it would be a diagnostic flourish dressed up as a metric, not a fact about the work.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>Why so much automation for a profile page?</b></summary>

<br>

Because the automation is the portfolio. This repository is a small, tested, self-verifying system with a twelve-workflow schedule, a commit serialiser, a hygiene scanner and a doctor — and it is durable proof that the same ideas work in a product. It is also the only place where I can show cron, Python, SVG and CI in one file tree.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>Two themes — why?</b></summary>

<br>

Because a dark sheet on a light page is a bad page. Each picture is drawn twice from one palette definition and served through `<picture>`, so it follows the visitor's system theme. Nobody has to flip a switch.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>What is this "feather fan" thing?</b></summary>

<br>

A homage to Florence Nightingale's 1858 army charts: when the data is counts in categories, draw the categories as bands whose thickness is the count. Here the bands are horizontal and give each repository its own wedge, with the automated share hatched — because the split between human and bot commits is the thing worth seeing at a glance.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>Can I steal the setup?</b></summary>

<br>

Yes. Copy `art/kit.py` and `art/build_all.py`, keep the palettes, drop what you don't need. The workflows are deliberately boring — `actions/checkout`, `setup-python`, one script, one commit script — so they can be lifted into any repository. See `.github/scripts/doctor.py` and copy the checks that catch your own mistakes first.

</details>
